AN EDITOR ASSASSINATED.
The Perils of Journalism in New Mexico.
SANTA FE, N. M., Dec. 27. — A. M. Conklin.
The Perils of Journalism in New Mexico.
SANTA FE, N. M., Dec. 27.—A. M. Conklin, editor of the Socorro Sun, was shot and killed on Christmas evening as he and his wife were leaving the Methodist church Christmas festival, by Jacob Baca, one of a prominent Mexican family. The deceased incurred the ill will of the Baca family in the Territorial Legislature by boldly expressed sentiments concerning education and the abuses of civil rights in the Territory. Some slight disturbance in the festival which Conklin as usher corrected, was the immediate cause of the murder. No justice of the peace can be found to arrest Baca, and there is great excitement in Socorro, which may lead to strife between the American and Mexican population.
The assailants of Conklin are guarded by 2000 Mexicans. A large posse of Americans well armed intend to get the murderer even if they have to fight for him.

FORT MONROE, December 28.—A disturbance occurred Friday at Smithville, fifteen miles west, between a white man named Dunn and a party of colored men who had met to organize a military company. One of the men caught Dunn by the whiskers and slapped his face, whereupon he drew a pistol and killed the negro. Dunn then ran into a store and loaded his pistol, when a crowd headed by Dan Cook with a drawn sword attacked him. He shot Cook dead, after which he drew a butcher knife and cut his way out. One man named Ed. Drew was badly cut in the abdomen and will probably die, while others were more or less injured. Dunn gave himself up and is now in jail. Intense excitement prevails among the colored people of the peninsula.

AN INHUMAN MOTHER.

BELLEVILLE, ILL., December 28.—A little settlement called Twist Hill, some eightor ten miles from here, was much excited Saturday morning last by the discovery of the dead body of Mrs. Sutter, a widow, lying in bed between her two children, little girls six and four years of age, and the dead body of an infant in a basket in a shed in the rear of the house. It appears that Mrs. Sutter was confined some time during Friday night, and that she placed the baby in an out-house, where it was frozen to death, and then returned to her bad and died from hemorrhage.

MYSTERIOUS ASSASSINATION.

GLENS FALLS, N. Y., December 28.—John Shaw, while sitting at the window of his residence last evening, was shot dead by an unknown assassin.

SHOOTING AT A DANCE.

DENVER, December 28.—A Republican special says: On Saturday night, during a drunken row in a dance hall at Robinson's Camp, a man named Meally was shot through the breast. Policeman Wm. Elbany, in attempting to arrest the disturbers, was shot in the foot. Several others had bullet holes in their clothing.

KENTUCKY KILLINGS.

MIDWAY, December 28.—Thede Lee shot and killed Chris. Lawson, his brother-in-law, on Christmas night, after being severely and dangerously stabbed by Lawson.

BARDSTOWN, December 28—An aged negro named Robert Nicholson, in a temporary rage, yesterday shot and killed Thomas Applegate, a lad 11 years old, who had offended him while visiting at his house.

A DESPERATE STATE OF AFFAIRS.

DENVER, December 28.—A Tribune Santa Fe special says: A very serious disturbance exists to-day at Socorro, New Mexico, the authorities refused to arrest the murderer of Conklin, editor of the Socorro Sun, and the citizens finding no recourse at law arrested and hold by force the Sheriff and four others, including the murderer of Conklin.

The rescue of the prisoners is threatened and bloodshed imminent. A request has been made to the military commander of the district for troops, and although the troops cannot be used as a posse comitatus, yet a company have been ordered from Colorado, N. M., as a means of protection for public property and the property of the R. R. Company. Bodies of men are being armed at Albuquerque and other points in the vicinity, and will go to Socorro to-night. Grave results may be expected to-night. All the women and children have been moved out of town.

SUICIDE OF A POSTAL CLERK.

St. Louis, December 28.—The dead body of Henry Tremyer, German, forty-seven years old, was found in the southern part of the city to-day with a bullet hole in the head, he having committed suicide. He was a clerk in the postoffice, and the only reason assigned for the act was the apprehension that he would be discharged. He left a wife and two children.

KILLED IN NEW MEXICO.
A. M. Conklin, For a Long Time Connected With the Sentinel,
Brutally Murdered on Christmas Eve by Three Mexicans.
A. M. Conklin Murdered.
Special to the Sentinel:
DENVER, Dec. 23.—The Republican's Socorro, N. M., special says: "At a Christmas festival held here on Christmas Eve, several Mexicans created a disturbance, which was quieted by A. M. Conklin, editor of the Sun. Shortly afterward, while Conklin and wife were leaving the church two Mexicans seized him by the arms, while a third fired three shots, killing Conklin instantly. His assailants fled to a small town in the vicinity, where they are guarded by 2,000 Mexicans. A large posse of Americans, well armed, intend to get the murderers if they have to fight for them."

RATON'S R VISHER. A Notorious Practitioner Barely Escapes Lynching.
"Dr." C. A. Washington of Raton City barely escaped lynching Wednesday night, and to voice public sentiment, "it is a pity he isn't hung." Washington is well known to the people of this region and enjoys anything but a good reputation. He has traveled all over the country, spending several years on the Pacific coast, engaged in what business we are unable to state. He is branded as a lustful wretch, who has brutally maltreated two women who have borne his name, and has caused many another, whom he has wronged, to become nearly heart broken.

His last victim was Miss Abbie J. Sinel, a respectable and by no means unattractive young woman of Topeka, Ks., who, being obliged to earn her own living and contribute to the support of a needy family, went to Raton City sometime in July or August. There she found employment as table girl in the Mountain House, which was disgraced by the presence of Washington as a boarder. Miss Sinel's pretty face roused the sensuous wretch and after finding his blandishments unable to accomplish his base purposes he sought to ruin the unprotected girl by the most debasing means. The opportunity presented itself when Miss Abbie was stricken down with fever and Washington, as the only physician in that region, was called in to attend her. The whole details of the fiendish crime of the monster are too revolting to dwell upon. Putting the young girl under the influence of chloroform, he sated his lustful cravings; and not only once, but as the poor girl in her misery stated, realizing the depth to which she had been dragged down, she was ravished on eight or ten different occasions by Washington. Her sickness became alarmingly dangerous, aggravated by the agony of mind which she suffered, and Wednesday night, before breathing her last, she told the revolting story of her shame and disgrace.

The people of Raton, as may easily be imagined were righteously indignant, and the thought of the poor girl lying dead, so incensed them that they forgot a moderation and a band of vigilantes was immediately formed and Washington's life hung in the balance.

Everything was made ready and lynching was only prevented by officer Hogan and a cow-boy, who espoused the cause of the brute, and hustled him off to Ctero.

The inquest over the body of Miss sincl was to have been held yesterday, and the utmost sympathy was expressed for her, and the most abject hate for Washington.

Washington, who bore the title of doctor, purchased the honor, or a diploma conferring it, from the Kansas City Medical College, where he attended lectures during the winter of 1877-8.

In 1876, after months of turmoil with his wife in La Veta, Colorado, he sought to kill her, and being frustrated in this, attempted to burn her alive by firing the house in which they lived. He was forced to flee the town, a mob threatening to hang him. He was carried to West Las Animas by George Ross, a colored man of unquestioned veracity of this city, who avers that but for a timely "lift" on the way, Washington would have dangled as a tassel to a hempen cord. Notwithstanding his narrow escape from lynching, he had the audacity to introduce himself into Masonic circles in Las Animas, but he was given the cold shoulder and after a two months' stay went to Kansas City.

In some way he obtained a devore from his wife and then succeeded in winning the band of Miss Menger, an estimable young lady, daughter of Dr Menger of Et Mra. He then began to practice in Otero, and was financially very successful. Mrs. Washington was a hard working woman and devotedly attached to her husband, receiving in exchange for her love and devotion, only kicks, blows and curses. The poor woman was most inhumanly treated and the result was premature labor; and she was finally forced to return to her father's house. To add to all the misery, she was branded by her husband with unfaithfulness and was well nigh driven into the grave.

Lost winter in Otero Washington had a difficulty with old man Dolton, and murdered him with a clasp knife. As Dolton had been a hard drinker, the "Dr." succeeded in establishing a plea of self defense and thus cheated the gallows.

Washington is a tall, spare, raw-boned six-footer, with black hair and beard, and long peaked face. He dresses in flashy style, and is impudence personified, always obtruding himself everywhere. It is to be hop-that his career is run and that he will pay the full penalty of the law.

ATTEMPTED ESCAPE. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. Quinov, Ill., Dec. 3.—To-day a number of prisoners confined in the County Jail made a bold attempt at escape. Six white men, during the absence of the attendants at the jail, picked up a large piece of timber in the hall and bent some of the iron rods in the gate separating them from the colored prisoners. The latter then squeezed through between the bent bars and joined the white men, and they unitedly made an assault upon the iron gates leading to the outside halls of the jail. After trying one in front of the jailer's room door on the east, they went to work on the one under the west porch of the Court-House, and had almost accomplished their purpose of freeing themselves when they were interrupted by the arrival of a young son of Sheriff Ording, who immediately gave an alarm, and the Sheriff secured all of his men in their colls. The prisoners had sent young Ording up into the city upon an errand before they began operations, expecting to be free when he returned. The timber they used as a battering ram was one kindly placed there by the Sheriff for them to sit upon when they were tired. ROBBED. Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune. Foster and James Galloway, Democrats, and Samuel Logan, colored Republican, the three Manchester, Va., election judges charged with refusing to receive the votes of a number of colored voters at the last election, on the ground of not having legal tax receipts, was concluded by the United States Commissioner to-day. HIT WITH AN AX.

LANSING, Mich., Dec. 3.—Two residents of this city, named Franklin W. Rice and John Cook, engaged in an altercation last night in regard to a pair of bars. Cook, an old man over 70 years of age, was knocking the bars down with an ax to lot his cow into a lot, when Rice ordered him to stop. A MURDEROUS NEGRO. BALTIMORE, Md., Dec. 4.—Intense excitement prevails in Baltimore County about ten miles east of this city in consequence of a murderous assault made on Joseph Woods, a farmer, by a negro named Gardner. He struck his victim with an ax, crushing his skull, and knocked down the wife while assisting her busband into the house. Gardner seized a gun near the door, and as soon as the door was shut on him fired through the lower part, the charge entering the groin and abdomen of Woods. Gardner was arrested, and is now in the County Jail, and in danger of being lynched.

DENVER, Colo., Dec. 4.—The Tribune's special says Dr. C. A. Washington was hanged by a mob at Otero, N. M., on Thursday night. He had treated a dining-room girl at the hotel, who died Wednesday, stating before her death that he had chloroformed her and taken improper liberties.

CANADA.

Toronto, Dec. 4.—Bertie Crawford, the second victim of yesterday morning's fire, uncumbed this forenoon to the injuries he received. The little fellow's sufferings were intense during the night, and his moanings were most heart-rending. In almost equal agony in the same room lay Mr. Crawford, who it was feared could not survive the night. At an early hour this morning he was much easier and able to converse, although his hearing was considerably affected, but during the day he suffered a relapse, and his life now hangs by a thread. He has not yet been informed of the death of his child, and, not hearing any more moans from it, frequently asks whether it is alive or dead. The four others who were more or less seriously injured are now progressing favorably and will recover. The origin of the fire is shrouded in mystery. Mrs. Crawford utterly repudiates the theory that the fire originated accidentally from the coal-stove, and says that this stove has been burning steadily ever since the cold weather set in. The night before the fire all the dampers were closed and a coal could not have dropped out upon the floor. In addition to this, the fanlight over the stove door was fastened down on Thursday night, and yet, in the morning the fire was first discovered by the smoke issuing through the fanlight, which must then have been open. Another curious circumstance is that when Mr. and Mrs. Crawford went to bed on Thursday night the wife had a purse in her jacket-pocket containing over $1,500. When they were frightened away by the flames they found this jacket, but the money was gone. It is impossible to say whether any of the stock was stolen, because the flames caused so much damage. But Mr. Crawford, who this morning was quite sensible and fully alive to the dreadful affair of yesterday morning, was firmly convinced that his premises were entered by a thief who stole the money, and perhaps some of the stock, and in order to secure a safe retreat by creating excitement and confusion, coolly and deliberately set fire to the building. The detectives have the matter in hand.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

TORONTO, Dec. 4.—Intelligence from Hanlan is to the effect that he insists upon having the championship of the world contested for on Toronto Bay. His coming match with Laycock will only be for the championship of England. Hanlan says he has really never rowed a first-class race on his native waters, and he would like to give his own people a show now. Toronto Bay, he says, is better adapted for sculling than any water in England; and he does not see, therefore, why, as long as he dwells on its shore and retains his present position, he should not stipulate that matches for the championship of the world should take place there.

Hanlan comes in ahead in the court as well as on the water. The suit brought by James Johnson, contractor, against Edward Hanlan to recover damage for loss incurred in an accident to the hotel on the Island, has been concluded in the Court of Chancery. Vice-Chancellor Blake heard the case, and, on summing up, dismissed the case, with costs against the plaintiff, against whom also the costs in the County Court will be carried. The suit arose through the blowing down of the frame of Hanlan's new hotel during a gale. His Lordship held that the evidence showed that the building was not properly stayed, and that it was top-heavy with lumber, placed there by plaintiff. The latter also asked for damage for wrongful dismissal by Hanlan; but his Lordship held that there was nothing in the contract to cover this. This case, while before the County Court, came near detaining Hanlan from going to England at the time stipulated. At Pulaski, Tenn., on Thursday, a negro was taken from the Court, after being sentenced to imprisonment, and hanged by the citizens.

Colonel Charles Potter, step-son, of ex-Governor Van Zandt, of Rhode Island, was killed by Greasers recently in Colorado. He was employed in the United States Geological survey.

Sheik Abdullah attacked the Persians near Urumiah and defeated them, after killing great numbers and capturing three guns. The Kurds are threatening an advance on Urumiuh.

Mrs. Lyman Jones, of Virginia Township, near Coshocton, Ohio, gave birth to triplets, two boys and one girl, the combined weight of the three being forty pounds. Mother and children doing well.

Should Greece percipitate war before spring there is little doubt that the chief Powers would speedily become involved, and it would be almost impossible for France and Germany to remain neutral.

In the case of First Lieutenant Wallace Tear, of the Twenty-fifth Infantry, sentenced to be dismissed from the service, the President has mitigated the sentence to forfeiture of rank and half pay for a year.

The general feeling among members of Congress in Washington seems to be that the session should be devoted exclusively to business, and to let politics have a rest. This finds expression among Republicans and Democrats alike.

Miss Alice Sivel died at Ratoon, N. M., last Wednesday, from an overdose of morphine, administered by Dr. C. A. Washington. She had been suffering from pneumonia. Washington was arrested, but discharged, when a mob took him from jail and hung him.

Louis Almon Meaker, the young man who confessed to murdering, in conjunction with his mother, his cousin, Alice Meaker, in April last, was sentenced by the Supreme Court at Montpelier. Vt., to be hanged at Windsor Prison on the second Friday in February.

The French Government has decided to propose to the Chamber of Deputies to sell the Crown jewels, as possessing no historical value. It is estimated that the sale would produce 5,000,000 francs, which would be devoted to extending and improving National Museums.

The application by Parnell, Biggar, T. D. Sullivan, Sexton and Dillon for a postponement of the State trials until January 25, on the ground that the date fixed will interfere with their Constitutional right to be present when Parliament meets, was refused by the Court, with costs.

Cromwell, a village near Lignonier, Ind., was visited by a conflagration on Saturday. Four frame buildings were burned, occupied by George W. Reid, grocer; Miller & Green, grocers and butchers; John R. McDonald, saloon, and George Bradel, shoemaker. Reid has $2,000 insurance and McDonald $5,000.

The Secretary of the Treasury has issued a circular to the holders of United States 6 per cent. registered bonds, issued under the act of February 8, 1861, commonly known as the 6's of 1880, that the interest on said bonds, due December 31, 1880, will be paid with the bonds upon the presentation of the bonds for redemption. No interest on that loan will be paid upon schedules.

The indictments for murder against George W. Eagle, Town Marshal at Washington, Ind.; James Payton and Lemuel Hairston, which were found by the last Grand Jury, have been nollied, and the case dropped, by the advice of the Prosecuting Attorney. The charges grew out of the killing of Perry Wilson, an innocent bystander in a political row at Washington during the campaign.

SCENES IN ALEXANDRIA.
Disgraceful Row at the Polls-Incidents of Election Day.
The streets of Alexandria presented some very lively scenes yesterday, all business except voting being suspended, and the election being the sole topic of conversation. At the third ward, the polling place of which is at the court-house, the scenes throughout the day were disgraceful in the extreme. Gangs of democratic roughs crowded into the line in front of the colored men, and would make their way as far as the window, then fall out, to again get into the line at another point and crowd out legitimate republican voters. About 3 o'clock in the afternoon it became evident that there would not be sufficient time to get all the votes in, as the polls were to close at sundown (5 o'clock). The democratic mayor, Mr. Cortland Smith, Mr. Chapman Neale, Alexander Hunter and other leaders were at the polling-place egging on their adherents, and on several occasions the line of voters was broken and republicans forced to fall back. The mayor sent for all the policemen in the city, who were soon on the ground. Two lines of voters were then formed of whites and colored. This did not mend the matter, and in a few moments the confusion was worse than ever. Major Burke here mounted a stand and urged the republicans to keep their temper and not disturb the peace. Chapman Neale harangued the democrats from the court-house steps, charging that 200 negroes had been sent to that polling-place to intimidate voters. The mob was now thoroughly enthused with bad whisky and the intemperate speech of Neale and ripe for a fight, which soon took place and was with difficulty suppressed. The other polling-places were comparatively quiet. About 100 voters, mostly republicans, were in line when the polls closed and were deprived of their vote thereby.

A row occurred in the Tontine restaurant, originating in politics, in which a gang of Washington Hancock men were the aggressors. They went to Alexandria for the purpose of serving the democracy in any capacity in which they might be called. Some of both parties were arrested. The officials at the station-house assured the Hancock men that they would be released that night. Gentlemen who carefully observed the proceedings state that the whole Alexandria police force, with one or two exceptions, were busily at work watching and challenging republican voters. A bold attempt was made by democrats to disfranchise a large number of republican voters who had paid the capitation tax and were entitled to vote, upon the ground that State-Auditor Massey appointed the tax-collector without the approval of Governor Holliday. Upon this the democrats expected to throw out several hundred votes, but the county judge of Alexandria decided that the tax-payers were not responsible for the neglect of the state officials, and the men were allowed to cast their votes. Several sailor repeators were allowed to vote and cast, as they said, "A slug for Hancock."

The scenes in the third ward were witnessed by many gentlemen from Washington, who denounce the shameful conduct of the democratic mob in the most emphatic terms. Men appeared in the crowd armed with double-barreled shotguns. A fence in the neighborhood of the court-house was stripped of its palings, which were used to arm the mob of democratic roughs. A number of colored men were seriously hurt in the melee, and one of them was stabbed in the side, but the result of his injury is not known.

WASHINGTON, NOV. 6, 1880.

Papers in the interest of the Southern Democracy are taking much pains to have the impression go abroad over the north that there was but little or no violence at the polls in the Southern states, and that the late election passed off peaceably. There being no voting in Washington, several gentlemen from this city went over to Alexandria to see how elections are conducted in Virginia. A CRUEL AND FOUL MURDER.
One of Our Oldest and Best Citizens Slain in Cold Blood Without Cause.
The Assassination of Mr. David Simmons by a Negro Named Granville Harrell.
The community was shocked Thursday morning by a report that Mr. David Simmons, residing near Jackson, had been foully and brutally murdered by a negro man in his employment named Granville Harrell. There had been scarcely an unpleasant word spoken by Mr. Simmons to the negro, and he was totally unconscious that he harbored a revengeful feeling towards him. While his back was turned towards the negro, the latter struck him a deadly blow on the head with an ax, and repeated it while he was down. The skull was crushed at each blow. After committing the deed, the negro went to the house and told the daughter of Mr. Simmons (the mother being absent) what he had done, and when reproached by the grief stricken daughter with tears and lamentation for killing her father, the fiend became furious and lifted his ax to strike her, but fortunately it was seized by his wife just in time to save her life. When arrested the murderer confessed, and boasted of what he had done, in language the most horrible and profane.

The following was the verdict of the jury of inquest:

We the jury, empanneled to sit on inquest over the body of David Simmons, Sr., find, after a full and careful examination, by the testimony submitted to us, that he came to his death by means of blows from an ax in the hands of Granville Harrell, and we believe that the said Granville Harrell is guilty of premeditated murder.

THE MURDERER.

Apprehending that the indignation of the community would overleap restraint, and lynch the assassin, Sheriff Morrison took the precaution to remove him early Thursday night from the jail here to the one at Raymond. We learn that on Saturday night a numerous body of persons, whose names to this writer are unknown, went to the Raymond jail, overpowered the jailer, seized the murderer and hung him. He repeated his confession, and at the same time made some statements implicating other parties which for prudential considerations we will not print.

MR. DAVID SIMMONS
the victim of this atrocious crime, was born in Germany on the 24th of April 1824. In his youth he immigrated to Jackson, where he has lived ever since. In 1846 he married Miss Denham, who, together with a family of sons and daughters, have survived him. There never lived a more upright, honorable man than David Simmons. He was kind to his family and just to everybody. He never gave offence, and would suffer wrong rather than engage in a quarrel. He was public-spirited, and loved to do charitable deeds. Fifteen orphan children were cared for and raised by him and his estimable wife. Without a moment's warning, he was deprived of his life on earth, but there is reason to hope that he has entered upon life of immortal bliss beyond the grave.

Mr. Simmons was buried with the honors which such a life as he had lived deserved. The Fire Department and an immense course of citizens followed his remains to the grave.

A Jackson telegram of the 19th to the New Orleans Picayune says: On Thursday evening, the 16th instant, one Granville Harrell, colored, murdered David Simmons, an old and respected citizen of this place. The fowl murder, it seems was unprovoked. Harrell was at once locked up in the county jail at this place. The sheriff, fearing mob violence, quietly took the prisoner to Raymond, eighteen miles west of here, where he was again confined, until last night, when a mob of fifty masked men overpowered the jailor, brought Harrell out and hung him to a tree a short distance from the jail. Harrell confessed his crime prior to the arrest, and boastingly said he cared nothing for the consequences.
granville-harrell-jackson-1880-12-18.A10:
A Fatal Locality.
The Raymond Gazette, in speaking of the spot where Granville Harrell was hung by a mob for the killing of Mr. Simmons, gives this bit of history:

In the year 1747, on the same road, not more than fifty yards below the tree on which Harrell was hung, Mr. J. W. Stewart, then Circuit Clerk of the county, was thrown from his horse and instantly killed. Fifty feet east of this spot in 1862 a negro was taken from from the jail and lynched in the same manner as Harrell. Two hundred yards south, nearer the town, in the field of Dr. Latimer, a mob shot and killed a negro, in 1866. Fifty feet west of this spot in 1875, a negro implicated in the famous Clinton riot, was taken from from the court house by unknown but infuriated parties and shot to death. Thus, in the same locality, no less than five different men have perished.
granville-harrell-jackson-1880-12-18.A11:
Swift Retribution.
Granville Harrell who murdered Mr. David Simmons last week with an ax, was unceremoniously taken from the jail at Raymond, last Saturday night, and hung by a body of about one hundred men. The Gazette brought to us yesterday a detail of particulars, and confession of the prisoner, in which he fully acknowledged his unmitigated guilt as the perpetrator of this horrible deed; but as our space is limited, and the whole account contains nothing more than what was embraced in our report last week, and Granville's confession here on the day of arrest, we deem it useless to publish more than the verdict of the Jury of inquest, which is as follows:

We the jury summoned on the inquest of Granville Harrell, a prisoner confined in the county jail, after hearing the testimony of the witnesses, found that he was taken from the county jail by a mob, estimated at from 75 to 100 unknown men, and found outside the corporate limits of the town of Raymond, near Snake Creek, hanging by the neck; and,

We further exonerate the Sheriff and his deputies, who were overpowered by the mob, and compelled to give up up the keys of the jail.

Sixty houses have been destroyed by floods at Limasol, Sicily.

The 23d of December was so dark in Pittsburg that the street lamps were lighted.

The Canadian census is to be taken on the first Monday in April, on the English plan.

There are 21,000 British troops in Ireland, and not a distinctively Irish regiment among them.

In London the weather is as warm as summer, while "violets are blooming in the gardens."

Two men, pleading guilty to sending lottery circulators through the mails, were sentenced in New York to pay a fine of $500 each.

Prof. Darwin, expounder of the evolution doctrine, is confined to his bed with bodily infirmities which may result in his death.

A Runaway team at East Bijou, Colorado, caused the death of John Hillson, one of the wealthiest and best known cattle men of the West.

Anderwert, the new President of the Swiss Republic, celebrated Christmas by shooting himself dead in the public promenade of Geneva.

A Fire in St. Louis destroyed the Pacific Flouring Mills valued at $100,000, and resulted in the death of a fireman named Carroll and the injury of two others.

A Later St. Petersburg dispatch says that the report of a scheme of the Government, implying the virtual abdication of the Czar, is absolutely unfounded.

A Paris cablegram says heavy floods are reported in the Department of Calvados. Several towns and villages are inundated, and houses have fallen in. The damage is considerable.

Jay Gould and his Cable Construction Company have ordered the manufacture of two Atlantic cables of the Siemens Brothers, of London, and preparations for their manufacture have already begun.

During a disturbance in the hotel of H. T. Griffin, at Rockaway Beach, one Mahon attempted to stab the proprietor. The latter drew a revolver and fired six times at Mahon, who fell mortally wounded. Griffin then seized a gun and riddled Mahon with buckshot.

The report of Public Printer Defrees shows an enormous increase in the Government printing business. There is not half room enough to store the printed matter as the printing progresses, and an enlargement of the building is recommended.

CHRISTMAS was a doleful day for the Oklahoma colonists. In addition to their bleak and uncomfortable surroundings, they received a dispatch from their delegate to Washington stating that the President refused to modify his proclamation against them in any way.

CHAS. D. SMITH, oldest son of Deacon Richard Smith, of the Cincinnati Gazette, died last week, of pulmonary disease. He graduated from Yale College in the class of 1863, and since that time has been on the Gazette staff. He was aged thirty-five years.

REV. SAMUEL B. CARPENTER, an Episcopal clergyman of Toledo, was forcibly robbed of a gold watch and $80 in money on a Lake Shore train, at Monroe, Mich., and while the amazed passengers were making up their minds what to do the thieves escaped.

MRS. MARION EVANS CROSS, the distinguished novelest known to the world as George Eliot, died December 22, of an affection of the larynx. She was first attacked on the 19th inst., previous to which time she was in good health and spirits. Her death was quiet and almost painless.

MARY FERGUSON, aged sixty-seven, of Brooklyn, N. Y., while washing, ran a pin into the forefinger of her right hand. The injured finger began swelling, and shortly after the swelling extended up the arm and over the body. She died three day after, the corpse turning perfectly black.

The relatives of a young lady named Eads, who died years ago in Pike County, Ind., have just recovered her skeleton from the office of a physician, where they had often seen it hanging. The doctors stole her body from the grave, dissected it, and put the skeleton on exhibition. Now some one in the secret discloses the shocking facts to the relatives.

Bank clearings increased to $1,693,000,000; grain receipts to 161,000,000 bushels; pork packing to 5,375,000 hogs slaughtered. Many manufacturing firms have doubled their trade, and prices are uniformly better.

GEN. R. K. Scott, who was Governor of South Carolina from 1889 to 1872, shot and killed a drug clerk named Warren Drury, at Napoleon. O., early Christmas morning. Scott's son, who had been on a spree, was given shelter and a bed by Drury. His father, learning of his whereabouts, attempted to go to him. Drury refused him admittance, whereupon Scott drew a revolver and shot the youth dead. Drury was to have been married, in Pittsburg, on the 27th of December.

Two vagrants, Barney Duffy and John Mahoney, lay down on the cinder carted from the Pacific Rolling Mill, at Paterson, N. J. Duffy was overcome with gas from the smouldering heap, and Mahoney made him coffee in an old tin can, and then procuring aid, carried him to St. Joseph's Hospital, near by. He then went back and lay down on the cinders, and was found in the morning dead and burned to a crisp, his toes being burned quite off. He had been suffocated, the wind having freshened in the night and fanned the cinders to a glow. The body, still burning, was found in the morning.

A TERRIFIC STORM.—We are told, that on Monday evening about 7 p. m., a cyclone passed through the Western and Northern portion of the parish doing a great deal of damage. Searcely a house was left standing on Mr. Joe and Mac Armstrong's places, two mules belonging to the former were killed, and one man on Mr. Mac Armstrong's place was killed outright. We have not been able to get the particulars of the damages and losses sustained by those gentlemen, nor have we heare what other damage has been done in that unfortunate neighborhood. We hope, however, nothing else serious was done.

Since writing the above we have seen Dr. Abbington from the upper portion of the parish, who tells us that he, together with Mr. Baily Lout, were in the house with the widow Trammel and her family, when the wind literally twisted and lifted it from off the sills and piled people, logs and furniture in one conglomerated heap. Strange to say, no one in the house sustained any serious injury. The cyclone was confined to a strip of country not more than half a mile wide but over this narrow strip it spread ruin and devastation, as it went. Dwellings, barns, fences and crops were blowed to atoms; men were snatched from the ground and hurled back with a force known only by those who have experienced the like. The adage "that one misfortune follows another," has been verified with us. The news of the storm and its ruins followed in the trail of Hancock's defeat.

LYNCHING IN SABINE.
The Shreveport Standard holds up its hands in holy horror at the cool account the Sabine Index gives of the lynching of two horse thieves, who were taken out of the Many jail and shot to death on the night of Nov. 11. We are told that this sort of thing is no rare occurrence in Sabine parish, not less than eight or ten alleged thieves having suffered the same fate within the last few years. We agree cordially with the Standard in condemnation of such occurrences, which are a shame and disgrace upon the good people of Sabine, and speak poorly for the civilization we profess to be governed by. Had such an underhanded measure taken place here in Grant the outcry would be loud against this "rioting parish." Thank heaven, the days of bloodshed and lawlessness are over, and Grant can point to a record for the past six or seven years that will do honor to any parish in the State. The law abiding citizens of Sabine should combine to put a stop to such occurrences, which, in this instance, as in all others, we are satisfied, a few hotheaded and irresponsible parties have committed, in opposition to the will and wishes of the bulk of those who have the peace and welfare of the community at heart.

Wife Murder—Judge Lynch Abroad.

BODIE, November 8th.—Job Draper was arrested Saturday for the brutal murder of his wife at a point on the road between Bodie and Mammoth City, and about four miles from Bodie. The couple had moved to this new location Friday, and had not yet provided themselves with a house. After building a fire of sage brush, Draper accused his wife of hiding his gun and a jug of whisky. Wood-choppers who were passing heard them disputing about the matter, but thinking it was only a drunken quarrel, moved on in the darkness. The following morning Draper went to a ranch and stated that his wife was dead, and accompanied two men to the scene. They found the body horribly bruised and cut. Her face was frightfully mangled. Draper was arrested, but says his wife came to her death by falling out of the wagon.

The citizens of Bridgeport and vicinity having formed themselves into a Vigilance Committee to hang T. E. Hawkins, who shot Henry Robbins a few nights ago, the prisoner was brought to Bodie for safe keeping; but as the citizens threatened to lynch him here, he was removed to Aurora. The shooting was cold-blooded, and Hawkins will not escape hanging if he is brought back to the County Jail.

Attempted Wife Murder and Successful Suicide.

FRESNO, November 8th.—M. C. Frietas, a barber of this place, fired a pistol shot at his wife, but failed to hit her. Immediately after the shot he took a dose of poison from which he died a few hours later. The parties were not living happily together, there being a suit for divorce pending between them. Jealousy was the cause.
